en: Preface to the *Record of Miraculous Responses to the Upholding of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: Śākyamuni attained Buddhahood already immeasurable kalpas ago;

however, solely out of his vow to deliver sentient beings, he manifested his appearance on the eighth day of the fourth month in the year of Jiayin during the reign of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty. He was born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and renounced the royal throne to leave the household.
The Master was born in his home on the eighth day of the twelfth month in his thirtieth year. At the time when the morning star appeared, he attained enlightenment.
He preached the Dharma for forty-nine years, delivering more than three hundred assemblies of sutras. His teachings were divided into five periods, all of which belong to the Mahāyāna.

Among them, the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Vajra*, and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* sutras constitute the most supreme vehicle of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Regarding the *Avataṃsaka*, it takes the principle that "the defiled is identical to the pure" as its foundation.

The *Vajracchedikā* takes as its central tenet the absence of marks and the non-apprehension of a single dharma; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* takes as its central tenet that every person shall attain Buddhahood.
If a student can thoroughly investigate the mind through these three sutras, the Buddha-dharma will be coextensive with their very chest. Master Lianchi said:
The *Avataṃsaka* possesses immeasurable gates; all other Mahāyāna sūtras are but a single gate among the immeasurable gates of the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Avataṃsaka* is the Heavenly King, while the various Mahāyāna sūtras are the feudal lords, and the various Hīnayāna sūtras are the vassal states of those lords.
Judging by these words, it is clear that this scripture is held in the highest esteem. Indeed, this scripture serves as a lamp for the world.

The primary truth (paramārtha-satya) spoken by the World-Honored One at the beginning: after the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment, he taught the Dharma by emitting light across seven locations and nine assemblies for the sake of the bodhisattvas.
Mañjuśrī, Ānanda, and others compiled these teachings on Mount Cakravāḍa, while the devas of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven and the nāgas all protected the treasury of the Dharma.
Consequently, the Bodhisattva [Nāgārjuna] sought out the secret scriptures in the Nāga palace, and the Great Sage Kātyāyanīputra...

That such a sublime and wondrous teaching as this has been transmitted to the Eastern Land—how fortunate we are to have heard it! Thus, by upholding even a single chapter, one already attains pure precepts;
by reciting a single verse, one can shatter the hells. Even a drop of water used for washing one’s hands is sufficient to rescue and sustain the lowliest of living beings;

how much more so, then, the acts of copying, reading, reciting, expounding, contemplating, and practicing, which communicate with the unseen realm and evoke profound resonance, transcending both the human and celestial realms. As it is said:

Is this not clearly recorded in various biographies? Having already compiled the two works on the miraculous responses of upholding the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, I have further selected the accounts of spiritual resonance from this sutra and set them forth to encourage future generations. Some may say that in the Mind-Teaching (*cittadharmatā*), there is no duality;
subject and object are both empty. Even the robe and bowl of Huangmei were intended to be cast aside as one side—how much more so, then, this [mere] distinction?
The regional records and biographies merely trace coarse traces; what connection do they have with Perfect Enlightenment?

Nevertheless, the great principles of the five periods all manifest cause and effect—what is called "the cause encompassing the ocean of fruition" and "the fruition penetrating the source of the cause. Within this compilation, the accounts of responsive miracles are presented in full detail, precisely conforming to this intent.
If, by means of these, the various capacities of beings may be stirred and right faith inspired, it will serve as a supreme incentive for diligent practice and cultivation.
One will naturally see one's nature and attain Buddhahood. Next, one should likewise gather in the sails from the sea of suffering and swiftly plant the seeds of the Buddha-cause.
Among the sages of antiquity, marvelous conditions were not lacking; indeed, there is truly no distinction between the ordinary and the holy.

Although it is as the ancients have said—that exotic birds carry flowers and the Sea King sends down rain, that earthquakes flow with the light of the Western Regions, and tigers tame themselves to carry the bowl of Taiyuan—the efficacy of these signs is clearly visible.
In the present day, how does the principle differ from that of the past? Furthermore, the sutras state that one should contemplate the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, for "all is created by mind alone.
Śākyamuni’s deliverance of sentient beings was likewise because every person possesses Buddha-nature; thus, the Buddha appeared in the world to deliver them.

Those who uphold the sutra need only prepare a single piece of sincere, refined mind, and the various sages and worthies of the Flower Treasury Adornment (*Huazang zhuangyan*) will appear before them.
If one can personally hear and personally see [the truth] throughout the kalpas in this manner, then perhaps one will not have failed the forty-nine years of bitter instruction.
Thus, may it be appropriate to take this principle as the unified explanation for the "holding and verifying" (*chí yàn*) found throughout the various sutras?
Compiled with Reverence by Zhou Kerufu, a Disciple of Pure Practice from Ancient Yangxian.
A Catalogue of Accounts of Efficacy in the Recitation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra Throughout Successive Dynasties.
By the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna of South India and the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu of India.

The Mother of Minister Zhengmo, Mingge Yi'an, who was a disciple of Chan Master Rong,
the Yuan Hua-yen Bodhisattva Jinsudashili, and who was well-versed in the clear and discerning teachings of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Exhorting the circulation of the *Avataṃsaka* and citing scriptural evidence for its efficacy:
wherever this scripture circulates, it constitutes a virtuous condition (*kuśala-pratyaya*). The resulting merit and retribution are immeasurable. Thus it is said:

"One who can transmit the Mahāyāna Dharma to a single person is equivalent to performing ten acts of goodness; one who transmits it to ten people is equivalent to performing a hundred acts of goodness; and one who transmits it to a person of great status [is equivalent to performing a thousand acts of goodness]."

For those who are great heroes and possess great power, [the merit] shall equal a thousand good deeds; for those who reprint and widely disseminate [this work], it shall equal ten thousand good deeds.
How much more so for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which transcends the cycle of birth and death, never regressing until one finally attains Buddhahood.
This exhortation for a single person to cultivate the Pure Land is, in fact, the accomplishment of one sentient being as a Buddha.
All who become Buddhas must necessarily deliver immeasurable sentient beings; those beings whom they deliver all originate with me. Thus, the karmic reward of this merit is truly inexhaustible.
Therefore, I desire to exhort all who see or hear this to broaden their minds through the [teachings of] the Buddha.

Take this mind as your own mind, so that every person may come to know it and be reborn entirely in the Pure Land. What Longshu has said should naturally be believed with earnest conviction as being free from error.
As for the two sutras, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Avataṃsaka*, they are the most supreme vehicles among the wondrous teachings spoken by the Buddha.

Regarding the Great Being Avalokiteśvara, who universally delivers the world, there is no land where he does not manifest; the accounts of how past worthies were moved by his response are recorded throughout history.

The significance of these matters is clear and manifest. I have compiled them individually to encourage the cultivation of practice. This is truly the most expedient gateway for those yet to come, serving as a bell and chime to awaken the future and a bridge and raft for those on the final path.
In the autumn of the Wuxu year, I compiled the *Records of Experiences in Holding the Vajra*, for which I have already provided a brief preface for circulation.
I now respectfully entreat my fellow practitioners to publish these records concerning the Pure Land, the Lotus Sūtra, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, and the holding of Avalokiteśvara.

I have searched through the archives and collected from ancient and modern records, exhausting the subtle labors of both mind and hand, so that my devotion might be directed toward something imperishable.
However, as the woodblocks for printing were produced here, they have not yet been widely disseminated to other provinces.

Since we all dwell together within this adorned Buddha-land, how could we allow for a deficiency in the excellence of the Dharma’s circulation? I therefore appeal once more to the virtuous faithful of the present age who may obtain [this work].
Having examined various editions, I have not been parsimonious in carving and distributing them widely.

Whether following the original texts or revising them into new compilations, I particularly hope that those who have encountered or heard these teachings, and who possess accounts of their efficacy in practice, will continue to collect and add such records hereafter. To offer a single verse of praise is to nurture a single root of virtue;
to stir a single thought of encouragement is to extinguish a single instance of karmic transgression. By means of this, the lineage shall be perpetuated.

The Buddha’s wisdom-life consists in benefiting oneself and others; this refers to the various deities who protect the Dharma. Having protected the treasure of the Dharma, they will certainly and unfailingly protect those who propagate the Dharma and carry its treasures.
In the past, the worthy ones created "pictorial guides" (*kōzō-zu*) to encourage people to practice *nien-fo*.

Later, when others were reborn in the Pure Land through much recitation of the Buddha's name, they attributed the merit to the person who had provided the pictorial guide, and that person also attained rebirth in the Pure Land.
The merit of the Dharma-gift is thus inconceivable. I pray that all fellow practitioners may together exhort one another.

*A Record of Experiences from Maintaining the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

From the Great Kingdom of South India: A Bhikṣu of great fame and virtue, styled Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, born of the Brahmin caste, of great nobility.
His noble family began when he was born beneath a tree; because he attained the Way through the aid of a dragon, this became his name.

During his infancy, he recited the four Vedas, consisting of forty thousand stanzas, all of which he understood with immediate clarity. Upon reaching the age of twenty, he gained renown throughout various kingdoms.

There was no aspect of astronomy, celestial phenomena, or other esoteric arts that he did not master. He formed a bond with three companions and entered the mountains, where they came upon a Buddhist stūpa. They emerged...
He made his home a place for the Way. For ninety days, he recited all the sutras and treatises existing in Jambudvīpa and attained complete mastery of them.

Thereupon, seeking further extraordinary scriptures, he headed toward the Snowy Mountains and saw a bhikṣu there who bestowed upon him the Mahāyāna teachings. He took great delight in reading and reciting them.
His eloquence was inexhaustible, and all who heard him were humbled and submitted, requesting him to serve as their teacher and model.
He then claimed for himself the status of an omniscient one (*sarvajña*) and gave rise to arrogance. Desiring to enter through the gate of Gautama, the gate deity said to Nāgārjuna:
"At present, your wisdom cannot yet be called capable of debate. Compared to the Tathāgata, you are no different from a firefly attempting to rival the radiance of the sun and moon. I observe...
"O Benevolent One, you do not possess omniscience; how can you wish to enter through this gate? When Nāgārjuna heard this, he was abashed and felt ashamed.
He thought to himself: "Within the worldly dharmas, the paths are infinite. Although the Buddha's sutras are subtle, their phrases and meanings are not exhaustive."
"I should now further expound upon this to awaken future students and to benefit all sentient beings. Having formed this thought, he stayed alone in a quiet chamber within a crystal palace.

Out of compassion for him, the Bodhisattva Mahānāga used his supernatural powers to transport him into the great ocean to his palace, where he opened a casket of the seven treasures and [retrieved] various profound and extensive sūtras of the Vaipulya class, immeasurable and wondrous.

The Dharma was transmitted to Nāgārjuna. Within ninety days, he attained a profound and thorough understanding. Knowing that he had realized the Way, the Dragon King sent him back, releasing him from the palace.
Originally, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was compiled by Mañjuśrī. Shortly after the Buddha passed into nirvana, heterodox paths flourished and there were few vessels capable of receiving the Mahāyāna;
thus, this sūtra was withdrawn into the Dragon King’s palace for over six hundred years. When Nāgārjuna went to the Dragon Palace, he beheld it.
This sutra alone is profound and subtle. It was only after being recited in the heart that it first began to be circulated in the world.
This is recorded in detail in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra-kathā*, the *Record of the Western Regions*, and various editions of the *Biographies of the Patriarchs of the Huayan School*.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu was a native of India. By nature, he possessed keen intelligence;

initially, he took the Hinayana as his field of study, and his sharp discernment and analytical power were as swift as a star-sharp sword. When his elder brother, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga, feigned illness, he summoned Vasubandhu and instructed him in the Mahayana teachings, saying:
"Before I pass away, read the scriptures in which I have trained. Vasubandhu then read the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Thereupon, he beheld the Dharma-realm of Vairocana and the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices; through this, faith and awakening arose within him, and he exclaimed:
"I should take a sharp sword and sever my own tongue, to clarify the fault of my previous praise of the Hīnayāna. His elder brother stopped him, saying:

"It is as when a person falls to the ground because of the earth, yet also rises from the ground. In the past, you used your tongue to disparage the Mahāyāna; now, you may use that very tongue to praise it."

He then entered the mountains and studied the Mahāyāna scriptures. He composed the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*. On the day the treatise was completed, the great earth shook everywhere and a brilliant light shone forth;
this is recorded in the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions).
The Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhī Fǎlǐng was devoted to the Mahāyāna and sacrificed his life in search of the Dharma.
He heard that more than two thousand li to the southeast of Khotan lay the kingdom of Kučā. According to the oral tradition of the king, the ruler venerated the Mahāyāna;
within the royal palace were the *Avataṃsaka*, *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, and *Mahāsaṃnipāta* sūtras, each consisting of one hundred thousand verses, which the king himself upheld and recited. Zhuang...
Having made solemn offerings, he set out with provisions and staff in hand, enduring a journey fraught with hardships until he reached the kingdom of Kūpana.

There, he prayed with utmost sincerity and succeeded in obtaining the first portion of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consisting of thirty-six thousand stanzas, which he brought back. This was the scripture translated during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
it marks the beginning of the *Avataṃsaka* entering the Eastern Land (China).
Buddhabhadra (whose name is translated as "Jue Xian" [Awakened Virtue]) was a Tripiṭaka Master from Northern India during the Jin dynasty.

He was a descendant of King Amṛtodana. Having lost both his parents in childhood, he entered the monastic order as a śrāmaṇera. By nature he was intelligent and quick-witted; he extensively mastered the various sūtras and attained a profound understanding of dhyāna and the vinaya.
He constantly aspired to travel to various regions to propagate the supreme Dharma. It happened that the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of the Yáoqín arrived in Kaśmīra.
He questioned the monks of that country as to who might be suitable to propagate the teachings in the eastern lands; they all replied that Huixian was the one.
The Master had previously received the practice of Chan from Buddhadasa (Fodaxian), who was at that time also in Jibin.

Buddhadasa said to Yan: "Huixian is the man capable of reviving the monastic community and proclaiming the True Dharma. Consequently, Yan earnestly requested that he come together with him to the Eastern Xia (China). The Master granted his consent.
Traveling for three years, he moved by day in concealment and by night, enduring every kind of peril before finally reaching Donglai Commandery.

Hearing that Kumārajīva was in Chang’an, he went there with great joy. He engaged in dialectical discussions with him and transmitted the methods of dhyāna meditation. Later, he traveled to Eastern Jin;
in the fourteenth year of the Yixi era, Meng Yi, the Prefect of Wu Commandery, and Chu Shudu, General of the Right Guard, [invited him to] a separate...
He constructed a pure chamber and invited [the master] to translate the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Master then, at Xie Sīkōng Temple (also known as Dàochǎng Temple;

this is the present-day Xīngyán Temple in Rùnjì Prefecture, so named because it flourished through the *Avataṃsaka*) in Yángzhōu, held the Sanskrit manuscript in his own hand and, together with more than a hundred śramaṇas, translated thirty-six thousand verses of the Sanskrit original into sixty scrolls of the Jin dynasty scripture (comprising thirty-four chapters and eight assemblies). He interpreted the text to harmonize with the underlying principles, ensuring a thorough understanding.
The words were perfectly exquisite. Sāman Dharma-yè transcribed them, while Huìyán and Huìguān polished the language. Thus, the Huá-yán Hall still exists at Dào-chǎng Monastery.
When the sutra was first being translated, two young boys dressed in blue would frequently appear in the pond in front of the hall.

Emerging from the pond, he held fragrant flowers in his hands, burned incense in the burner, and poured water, never leaving the vicinity of his seat. As evening approached, he returned and submerged himself within the pool;
this was witnessed by the entire assembly. Because he had long resided in the Dragon Palace, the Dragon King, moved by joy and inspiration, caused his son to serve him.
Furthermore, there were benevolent deities who protected his attendants. Later, he entered Mount Lu and joined the community of Huiyuan.
Master Ye established the Lotus Society and translated various sutras on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha. He passed away in the sixth year of the Yongjia era at the age of seventy-one.
By folding three fingers of his hand, he demonstrated that he had attained the fruit of Anāgāmin. Master Ye’s character was elegant and refined; he had extensively studied all the various teachings.

He considered himself unable to fathom the subtle or illuminate the ultimate, and was constantly dissatisfied with his own lack of realization. Later, he encountered Buddhabhadra and requested that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* be translated.

Over several years, he consulted him on its principles and meanings until he attained a profound and comprehensive awakening. Looking at his friends, he said, "The compass for the holy teachings lies right here.
He subsequently propagated its profound tenets and became the preeminent leader of the school. He authored the two-fascicle *Zhiguī* (The Return to the Ultimate Meaning). [Huiyan and Hui]...
His calligraphy was lofty and simple, and his mastery of the sutras and treatises was profound and vast; he was one of the "Eight Talents" of Master Kumārajīva.
A śrāmaṇera named Prajñāmiga from the kingdom of Khotan strictly maintained his observance of the precepts and specialized in reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Suddenly, a person appeared before him with palms joined and said, "The devas have sent me to invite you, Master. Please close your eyes. In an instant, they arrived in the heavens.
The Lord of Devas knelt and entreated him, saying: "Now the various devas are engaged in battle with the asuras, having repeatedly suffered defeat and humiliation.
We beg you, Master, to recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and hope that you will provide protection through the power of the Dharma. The Master complied with his request;
mounting a celestial jeweled carriage and holding a heavenly banner and pennant, he focused his mind on the Avataṃsaka. With the host of devas facing those powerful enemies, the asuras suddenly—
The [fragrance] dispersed. After a short while, he was sent back; his body was imbued with a celestial fragrance that did not fade for the rest of his life.
Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty—translated as "Virtuous Merit" (Gōngdéxián)—was a native of Central India. Initially, he mastered the treatises of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*);
later, he delved deeply into the Tripiṭaka and advanced to the study of the Mahāyāna. His teacher ordered him to search through a case of scriptures, whereupon he immediately found the *Avataṃsaka*.
Yan was delighted by this and ordered him to give further lectures. During the Yuanjia era, he arrived in Guangzhou. The Regional Inspector, Che Lang, memorialized the throne;
Emperor Wen then dispatched an envoy to welcome him. Prince Yixuan of Nanzhao and others all took him as their teacher.

The Prince assembled over seven hundred śramaṇas specializing in the study of meaning, intending to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. However, because the Master had not yet mastered the Chinese language, he felt deep shame.
He sighed in lamentation. Thereupon, he performed prostrations and repentance morning and evening, reverently praying to Avalokiteśvara to seek a divine response.

He subsequently dreamed of a divine being who, holding a sword, took a human head and exchanged it for another. Upon waking, he felt a sudden clarity; from then on, there was no spoken Chinese language that he could not understand.
He then lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for ten or more times, and those who listened were completely won over and filled with admiration.

When the Master first arrived in Jianye, the Emperor asked him, "I wish to observe the precepts and refrain from killing; however, as the sovereign of the state, I am unable to follow this aspiration. What should I do? The Master replied:
The cultivation practiced by an emperor differs from that of an ordinary man. An ordinary man is of humble station and inferior reputation; he must therefore subdue himself and toil his body.
An emperor, however, takes the four seas as his home and the myriad people as his children. When he utters a single virtuous word, both officials and commoners rejoice;

when he promulgates a single benevolent policy, humans and spirits are brought into harmony. When punishments do not cause untimely deaths and corvée labor does not exhaust strength, then wind and rain will arrive at their proper seasons.
Frost and heat are regulated; the hundred grains flourish. To observe the fast in such a manner—how great the fast is! To refrain from killing in such a manner—how supreme the precept is!
Why must one wait until one has omitted a single meal for a time and saved the life of a single bird before it can be called a vast salvation?
The Emperor struck his desk in praise and issued an edict for the relevant authorities to provide him with all necessary supplies; the entire nation venerated him.

The Qi monk Huiguang resided in Luoyang and composed commentaries on the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Nirvāṇa*, and the *Daśabhūmika* sūtras, which perfectly exhausted the profound meaning of the provisional and the ultimate.
One day, while he was ill, he saw a host of celestial beings coming to welcome him. Huiguang said, "My vow is to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) alone."
Shortly thereafter, transformation Buddhas of the Pure Land filled the void. The light said, "I pray only that our Buddha may accept me and fulfill my original vow.
He then snapped his fingers and cleared his throat, after which both his speech and breath ceased. This is recorded in the *Wangsheng ji* (Collection on Rebirth) of Yunqi.

Vimalamati (魏 勒那摩提), whose name means "Jewel-Mind" in the language of China, was a native of Central India. He was widely read and possessed vast learning, and he clearly realized the principles of dhyāna.
At the beginning of the Zhengshi era, he arrived in Luoyang and translated twenty-four fascicles of treatises, including the *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*.

The Master’s mastery of the Chinese language and his extraordinary wisdom were beyond compare; the Emperor frequently ordered him to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, and his refined insights were brilliantly inspired. He once occupied the high seat [to preach].

Suddenly, there appeared those holding ceremonial tablets and carrying invitations, appearing like high-ranking officials, who said: "The Heavenly Emperor has come to invite the Dharma Master to lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The *dujiang* and *weina* all entreated him to attend. At that time, the assembly of monks at the lecture hall saw this together.
The Master smiled serenely, bid farewell to the multitude, and passed away upon his Dharma seat. The *dujiang* and other monks likewise entered [nirvana] simultaneously.
[He] attained extinction. Contemplating this, one knows that the secret treasury of the *Avataṃsaka* is thus revered by devas and humans alike.
The monk Fabian of Wei and Shu was exceptionally eminent in his practice of dhyāna; he had long maintained the *Avataṃsaka*.
At that time, when Prince Wuling marched eastward, he ordered his younger brother Gui to guard Yizhou. When the Wei general Wuchiwei Huai arrived to invade Shu, Gui surrendered. The city—
Those within were called monks, all of whom were under confinement. At night, suddenly a brilliant light illuminated the heavens. Daoheng dispatched people to search for the source of the light;
they found that while all the other monks were asleep, only the Master sat upright reciting a sutra. The light emanated from his mouth.

Upon hearing this, Daoheng went in person to the Master’s quarters, prostrated himself, and sat to listen until dawn before finally ceasing. He then asked the Dharma Master, "What sutra did you recite last night? The Master replied:

Daohui asked, "How much of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* have you been able to recite? The Master replied, "I, a poor monk, resolved to recite one entire collection (*piṭaka*), but due to much indolence, I have only now managed a thousand scrolls.
Daohui was struck with astonishment and doubt, unable to believe him. Wishing to test him, he said, "Would you be so kind as to recite it once?
Would it not cause you any fatigue or strain? The Master replied, "Reciting the sūtras is the constant duty of a śramaṇa; how could I dread such toil?"
He then prepared a high seat and ordered the assembly of monks to each hold a copy of the scripture, listening as the Master ascended the seat to recite it.
After seven days and nights, the count was complete. He rose from his seat to express his gratitude and take his leave, and consequently released all the monks. Thereupon, he sighed and said:
"Since the passing of the Tathāgata, Ānanda has been the foremost in dhāraṇī-retention; none have surpassed him. Yet here in Shu, there is such a person."
That he was thus constantly protected and brought peace and joy—how could this have been by mere chance? This is seen in the *Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks*.
The Śramaṇa Lingbian of the Later Wei dynasty was a native of Jinyang. Having planted superior roots of goodness in past lives, he regularly read the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Upon seeing the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, his reverence and study of it redoubled. He then carried this sūtra upon his head and entered the Qingliang Mountain Temple to seek Mañjuśrī.

He practiced in secret for years, prostrating himself until his feet were split and bleeding, his flesh wasted away and his bones exposed. Suddenly, he heard a voice from the air saying, "Cease for now;
simply contemplate this sutra with a focused mind, and you will naturally find the point of entry. The Master then opened the scroll and attained a sudden, great awakening.

In the first month of the first year of the Xiping era, he composed the *Huayan Lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka), expounding its meaning and explaining its text, exhausting its subtleties and penetrating its profound mysteries.
It consists of one hundred fascicles and has been circulated in the world.
The monk De-yuan was a native of Tian-shui; he constantly took the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice, reciting, chanting, and upholding it.

He subsequently cultivated a pure garden, planting various grains and mulberry trees, as well as fragrant herbs interspersed with fresh flowers. Every time he entered the garden, he would invariably perform a ritual washing.
They were washed, and their bodies clad in pure garments; they were sprinkled with fragrant water. The *zhǔ* tree had grown for three years, its fragrance pervading the four directions.

A separate chamber was constructed, its floor smeared with scented mud. The artisans were required to observe the fasts and change into clean robes; whenever they entered or exited, they must wash, rinse, and burn incense. The bark was stripped from the *zhǔ* trees and soaked in aloeswood (*agaru*).
After being boiled and purified, the paper was made, taking a full year to complete. A separate, pure foundation was then built to construct [the hall].

The New Chamber: Within the hall, square seats made of cypress wood were arranged, upon which incense and flowers were laid out. A precious canopy was suspended above, from which various tinkling pendants hung down.
White sandalwood and purple agalloch were used for the scripture tables and also served as pen-holders. Those who transcribed the scriptures received the *zhāijì* (fasting and precept-taking) daily.

Having bathed three times in fragrant water, wearing a flower crown and pure robes, and about to enter the scripture chamber, incense must be burned along both sides of the path, with a *bhāṣya* chant leading the way.
The master likewise dresses in solemn and clean attire, respectfully guiding the way while holding an incense burner and scattering flowers as an offering; only then does he begin the transcription.

Furthermore, the master kneels in the *hu-gui* posture, directing his thoughts, fixing his gaze, and inclining his heart. As soon as he has written a few lines, each character emits radiance, illuminating—
He occupied a single hall for a long time before finally resting. Again, a divine being appeared, holding a halberd and standing guard;
Yuan and the scholar saw him together, while the others did not see him. Furthermore, there was a blue-robed Buddhist youth who held celestial flowers in his hands as an offering.
After two years, when the transcription was complete, he placed it in a fragrant casket and set it within a precious canopy, where he paid homage with prostrations every day. Afterwards—
When it was recited, the case emitted a strange light. This scripture has been transmitted down to the present through five generations.

Whenever there is a pure reciter, spiritual responses manifest clearly at that time. It is currently still in the possession of Dharma Master Xianshou of West Taiyuan; see Huìhuì’s *Xuánjì* for details.
Later Wei’s Prince Yanming of Anfeng and Prince Yuanxi of Zhongshan were both eminent and virtuous members of the imperial clan whose resolve was unsurpassed.
Bowing their heads to the Perfect Teaching, they once used incense mixed with ink to transcribe one hundred copies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and one copy of the *Golden-Letter Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
These were all stored in cases made of the five fragrant woods and kept within caskets of the seven precious gems. On tranquil nights and auspicious occasions, they maintained a pure fast.
While practicing the Way, he immediately emitted divine light of five colors that illuminated the halls and pavilions; the multitude witnessed this together.
In the first year of the Wenming era of the Later Wei dynasty, Wang Minggan of Jingzhao fell into a state of unconsciousness due to illness.
He was led by two men to hell, and upon reaching the gate, he saw a monk who claimed to be Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. The Bodhisattva instructed him to recite a verse, saying: "If..."
"One who wishes to understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time should contemplate in this way: 'The mind creates all Tathāgatas. (This verse is from the Jin translation.
One who recites this verse can dispel the various sufferings of hell. Because Gan recited it, he entered the presence of the King.
The King asked, "What merit do you possess? He replied, "I have merely upheld a four-line verse. Thereupon, he recited it aloud as before.
The king then released him. While he was reciting the verse, all those suffering in the prison who heard the sound attained liberation.

After three days, Gan regained consciousness; remembering and upholding this verse, he recounted it to others, only then realizing it was from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, spoken by immeasurable bodhisattvas gathered in the Yāma Heaven Palace—specifically, the verse of Bodhisattva Jñānākara.
The latter two lines of the current *Tángjīng* (Sūtra from the Tang) state: "One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm; all things are created solely by the mind.

Although the phrasing differs slightly, the general meaning is the same. Since the merit of a single verse can destroy the hells, how much more so the profound subtlety of an entire fascicle or a whole volume!
This is seen in the *Zuǎnlíngjì*.
Liu Qianzhi, a eunuch of the Northern Palace, lamented his own status as one castrated by the law and turned his heart toward the Buddha Vehicle.
During the Tahe era, the Second Prince sought Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva at Mount Qingliang and made an offering by burning his own body.

Witnessing this event, Qianzhi submitted a petition requesting to enter the mountains to cultivate the Way. Carrying a copy of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he practiced with diligent devotion day and night, performing prostrations.

He performed repentance rituals and recited the scriptures, praying in his heart for sublime awakening. For twenty-one days, he abstained from grain and subsisted only on water. Although his physical strength and breath were diminished, his sincere devotion grew ever more earnest.

Suddenly, his beard and mustache grew back completely, restoring him to the appearance of a man; his spirit and countenance became clear and enlightened, and he thoroughly understood the profound meaning of the teachings.
He then devoted himself entirely to composing this scripture and its treatises, totaling six hundred fascicles, which he presented to the Emperor. The High Ancestor redoubled his reverence and faith.
The Avataṃsaka teaching flourished greatly at this time.
During the Sui dynasty, the monk Huiwu of the Chan-ding Monastery was a native of Jingzhao. He once lived in seclusion with another monk, Daoxiang, on Mount Zhongnan.

The Master upheld the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, while Daoxiang upheld the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. Subsisting on wild fruits and dwelling among the crags, each devoted himself exclusively to his own practice. Suddenly—
A man came to pay his respects, prostrating and inquiring after their well-being, saying, "I request one master to come to my residence for a vegetarian feast. The two monks deferred to one another.
The man said, "I request the Master who recites the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Wuyin followed him there; it was the abode of a mountain deity. He had invited a thousand arhats.
They all deferred to the Master as the senior monk. When the meal was finished, they all flew away through the air. The spirit summoned a young boy to serve him;
the boy immediately obeyed the command and said to the Master, "Please open your mouth. Once he had looked into the Master's mouth, he said, "The Master has a great illness.
The boy took the dirt from his fingernails and threw it into the Master's mouth. After a short while, he again ordered the Master to open his mouth and look at it, saying, "The illness..."
Having nearly finished the recitation, [the deity] leaped up and flew into his mouth. The child was indeed the essence of the medicine; the Master subsequently attained supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
He returned to his chamber to retrieve the scriptures and took leave of Daoxiang, departing by traversing the void into the distance.
The Sui dynasty monk Shi Linggan, surnamed Li, was a native of Didu. He left the household life under Dharma Master Yan. At the age of eighteen, he was able to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
He resided at Xingshan Monastery and served as a śramaṇa for verifying the meaning of translated scriptures. Later, he fell ill and died; after several days, he revived and said:
"I went to Tuṣita Heaven and saw the two Dharma Masters Hui and Yuan, both seated upon lotus pedestals, their radiance surpassing that of this world."
He said to Gan: "Inform my disciples on my behalf that they shall all be reborn here in the future. The Master’s aspiration was to uphold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

he constantly practiced the visualization of the Flower Treasury (*Huazang guan*) and the visualization of Maitreya’s Tuṣita Heaven according to the sūtras. When his illness became severe, his eyes gazed upward as if seeing something.
When the monk Tongzhen questioned him, he replied: "Just now I saw a youth dressed in blue robes lead me to Tuṣita."
"Divine pleasures are not lasting; in the end, one falls back into saṃsāra. The Lotus Treasury is my true aspiration. Shortly thereafter, his breath ceased, but he revived after a moment.
Zhen asked again, "What do you see now? He replied, "I see a great body of water filling everywhere, with lotuses as large as chariot wheels, and I am sitting upon one of them.
My wish is fulfilled. Having finished speaking, he passed away.
The Vinaya Master Tangyuan was a monk of Yanxing Temple in Jingzhao. At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, while traveling across the Bashi Bridge at twilight, he stayed overnight at an inn.

Suddenly, a strange monk arrived; his appearance and clothing were coarse and tattered. He took up residence in a separate room belonging to the host and proceeded to take fine wine and excellent meat, drinking and eating them with great relish.
The Vinaya Master, being pure in his observance of the precepts, was suddenly filled with loathing for this. That monk ate...
Having finished, he sought water to rinse his mouth, closed the door, sat upright, and recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra. First he set forth the title of the chapters;
next, as he recited, "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha," light emanated from both corners of the monk's mouth.
It was like the color of gold. By the third watch, four fascicles were nearly complete, and the light from his mouth grew even more intense.

After the fifth fascicle, the light gradually withdrew and re-entered the monk’s mouth. Before the fifth watch had passed, he finished reciting the sixth fascicle (that is, the entire sixty-fascicle Jin translation).
The monk then lay down again, while the Vinaya Master listened intently to the profound sound; he straightened his body in shame, with grief and remorse mingling in his heart.
At dawn, he entered the room to perform prostrations and repentance. When asked his name, he did not answer. After they parted ways, no one knew where he had gone.
The *Ganyingzhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance) states that while recording these accounts of resonance, there happened to be a madman nearby who asked: "I do not abstain from wine or meat."
"Is it possible for you to emulate that divine monk by reciting the Avataṃsaka Sūtra?
He replied, "Can you complete six fascicles of the scripture in a single night before the fifth watch? Can you emit light from your mouth while reciting at night to serve as a lamp?
Can you, like the Wine Immortal eating shrimp or Master Zhì eating pigeons, spit them out and have them return to life? You cannot do any of these things."
"You are capable indeed! To falsely imitate the deeds of divine monks and deceive the sages and worthies—your sin is as deep as the vast ocean; how could you possibly escape it?
Thereupon, the madman apologized with shame and withdrew.
Master Deyue of the Tang dynasty was surnamed Xing and was a native of Wutai County in Daizhou. He entered the monastic order at the age of seven.

Initially, he followed Chan Master Huichao to inquire into the practice of meditative concentration; Huichao held him in high esteem and addressed the assembly, saying, "Deyue’s cultivation is harmonious and luminous;
he is beyond the reach of those like you. Before long, he attained great awakening. Later, he resided at Foguang Temple to the southwest of Wutai.

He established a vihāra and specialized in the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Furthermore, following the sūtra, he practiced the visualization of the Buddha’s radiance (*buddhaprabhā-samādhi*).
He frequently went to Dafu Temple seeking a vision of Mañjuśrī. On one occasion, Mañjuśrī appeared before him and said, "There is no need for you to pay homage to me now;

you should instead reproach yourself. You will surely attain great awakening. Later, through this introspective inquiry, he realized non-arising (*anutpāda*) and simultaneously attained the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). Consequently, he felt a profound resolve to propagate and save others.
He prayed with sincerity to the Great Awakened One, requesting that his mind be witnessed. Moved by this, the Buddhas appeared and spoke a verse for him, saying:
"The Buddhas have attained the profound Dharma of quiescence through cultivation over vast eons;

if one can open and clarify this eye of Dharma, all Buddhas will rejoice. The Master further asked: "Can the Dharma of quiescence within emptiness be explained so as to teach others? All [the Buddhas]...
The Buddha then vanished. Only a voice was heard, announcing: "Skillful means and wisdom serve as the lamp; they illuminate the realm of the mind.
If one seeks to investigate the true Dharma, nothing at all is seen. Furthermore, the Prefectural Governor of his home province invited him to transmit the incense and confer the precepts.

Once his mission of transformation was complete and he was about to return eastward, the governor and the assembly escorted him to the east of the city. As evening fell, he wished to burn incense, when suddenly—
One heard a voice from the sky above the city saying: "Joining the palms serves as flowers; the body itself is the vessel of offering.
A virtuous mind is the true fragrance; the incense of praise spreads abroad. When the Buddhas smell this fragrance, they follow the sound to come and deliver us.
All you people, exert yourselves with diligence; never again shall you fall into doubt or error. Thus, the ancient tradition records the title: "Verses Praising the Array in the Void."
The Tang dynasty monk Shi Facheng, surnamed Fan, was a native of Yongzhou. He entered the monastic order in his youth and made the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* his daily practice.

Having encountered Chan Master Huichao, he lived in seclusion at Langu Valley. Later, on the southern ridges, he constructed an *Avataṃsaka* Hall, which he prepared with the utmost solemnity and purity.

He then commissioned paintings of the seven locations and nine assemblies of this very sutra and invited Zhang Jing, a calligrapher from the Hongwen Hall, to reverently transcribe the complete scripture.

The Master personally held the incense burner, single-mindedly offering worship with focused devotion. Suddenly, he beheld an auspicious bird of extraordinary form and color, which entered the room carrying flowers, circling about as an offering. At that time, it was considered a manifestation moved by his refined sincerity.
The monk Biancai served Dharma Master Yu from his youth. Daily, he devoted himself solely to the study of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, yet after a long time, he had not attained realization.

He then reverently fashioned a fragrant casket to hold the scripture and carried it upon his head while practicing the Way. After three years, in a dream, Samantabhadra instructed him on the profound meaning of the text;
suddenly, he could recite it by heart, as clearly as if looking into a mirror.

The Tang dynasty monk Fākong was a Langjiang of Yanmen during the late Sui period. He left his home and retired to a deep valley at Mount Qingliang, where he constantly recited the verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"The mind alone creates the Buddha. Later, he encountered a strange monk who transmitted to him the profound essence of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

His mind became suddenly empty and vast. When his end approached, he passed away while sitting upright. This account is found in the *Yunqi Ganying Lueji* (Brief Record of Miraculous Responses at Yunqi).
The monk Śīlagupta was a native of Siṃhala. Having realized the third fruit of the path, he arrived in China at the beginning of the Lín-dé era.
Emperor Gāozōng treated him with the utmost reverence. Later, he traveled to Qīngliáng to pay homage to Mañjuśrī, and from there proceeded to Xītāiyuán Temple.
At that time, it happened that the monks were reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The Master asked, "What sūtra is this? They replied, "The *Avataṃsaka*.

The Master’s countenance changed solemnly, and he said, "I did not expect to find such a sūtra even here in this land. He joined his palms in praise for a long while and said, "The merit of the Buddha in this Great Vaipulya [Sūtra] is inconceivable.
It is transmitted in the Western Regions that when someone reads this sūtra, they use water to wash their hands."

When insects and ants were moistened by the water, those that lost their lives were all reborn in the heavens; how much more so for those who receive, uphold, read, recite, and diligently contemplate [this teaching]?
The Tang dynasty Master Du Shun was surnamed Du and named Fashun. A native of Duling in Jingzhao, his conduct was lofty and pure.

He studied under no fixed teacher, devoting himself exclusively to the *Avataṃsaka* as his primary discipline. During his childhood, he preached the Dharma for the masses atop a burial mound behind his home;
all who heard him were awakened to the Mahāyāna. To this day, the "Dharma-preaching Mound" remains there. Furthermore, at Mount Zhongnan...
He compiled the essential meanings expounded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and composed the "Treatise on the Contemplation of the Dharma-realm" (*Fajie guanwen*).

At that time, he was moved by the Bodhisattvas of the Ocean-like Assembly, who manifested themselves to offer praise. Once the work was completed, he gathered fire to burn it; yet, as it perfectly accorded with the holy mind, not a single character was damaged.

While dwelling in the mountains, he once wished to plant sunflowers, but the ground was infested with many insects and ants. The Master then circled the boundaries to demarcate the plots, whereupon the insects immediately migrated outside. From this, he began his cultivation.

He cleared the land, and not a single thing was damaged. In Sanyuan County, there was a man who had been deaf and mute since birth; when the Master summoned him and spoke with him, his speech was restored as soon as he responded.
Thereafter, the Master went to the South Mountain and encountered the flooding of the Hengqu River; he halted the flow of the water and crossed over it by walking slowly.
On the day he was about to pass away, his assembly of those with whom he shared karmic affinity gathered; his voice and countenance remained unchanged as he entered stillness with serene detachment.
He was buried on the northern plain of Fanchuan; today, his entire-body stupa stands at Huayan Monastery south of Chang’an. According to the *Biézhuàn*, he was an emanation of Mañjuśrī.

In the first year of the Zhengsheng era (695 CE), on the fourteenth day of the third month, the day of Xinyou, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda—whose name in Chinese means "Delightful Learning"—from the Kingdom of Khotan in the Tang dynasty, began a revised translation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Foshouji Monastery in the Eastern Capital.

By the eighth day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shengli era (699 CE), the translation of the new scripture was completed. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this work is titled the *Acintya-sūtra*.
It consists of one hundred thousand verses. The *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) translated during the Liang dynasty is also called the *Baiqian jing* (Sūtra of One Hundred Thousand [Verses]).

The earlier translation produced during the Jin dynasty contained only thirty-six thousand verses—what is known as the "half-jewel" version of Dharmakṣema. At that time, an envoy was dispatched to Khotan to welcome the Sanskrit manuscript to China.
The Master translated it once more, supplementing the omissions of the previous version by adding nine thousand stanzas;

thus, including the original, the total reached forty-five thousand stanzas, forming eighty fascicles (in thirty-nine chapters and nine assemblies) for the Chinese edition. Tradition states that among the ten categories of scriptures possessed by Dharmakṣema, this is the first:
the *Saṃkṣipta-sūtra* (Abridged Version). Both current translations are abridgments from within the hundred-thousand-verse original, as the full translation had not yet been completed.
Because it was complete. However, regarding the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang Shijie*) described in the first assembly, the Jin edition was largely deficient;
it was only upon reaching the eightieth fascicle that it became fully intelligible and was presented in its brilliant entirety.
At that time, the Great Virtuous Tripiṭaka Master Yijing, Zen Master Hongjing, and the Dharma Masters Yuanze, Shenying, Fabao, and Xianshou, along with Dharma Master Fuli, jointly translated it.
Composition of the Text: From the initial translation on the day of Xinyou, one day later on the day of Renshu, there was a response in the form of a descent of sweet rain from heaven.
The Tang monk Fazang, styled Xianshou, was of the secular surname Kang and was a native of the country of Kangju. Initially, his mother conceived him after dreaming of a wondrous light;
upon his birth, he aspired to the Unsurpassed [Vehicle]. Later, Master Yan lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Yunhua Monastery.
At the monastery, when the Master arrived at midnight, he suddenly saw a divine light come to illuminate the courtyard and buildings.

He sighed and said, "There shall be an extraordinary person who will propagate the vast and great teaching. When morning came, he encountered Master Yan; from then on, he devoted himself to him and delved deeply into the inexhaustible [Dharma].

In the tenth month of the second year of the Shengli era, the newly translated *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was completed. By imperial decree, the Master was ordered to lecture upon it at Foshouji Monastery. Ten...

On the twelfth day of the second month, while he was lecturing on the "Chapter on the Realm of the Flower Treasury" (*Huazang Dijie Pin*), the lecture hall and the ground within the monastery suddenly shook.
Thousands of monastics and laypeople witnessed this together and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He subsequently gave a public lecture at Yunhua Monastery.
A white light issued from his mouth and, in an instant, formed a canopy; the multitude of ten thousand people leaped for joy.

Previously, in the first year of the Zongzhang era, a Tripiṭaka master from the Western Regions had arrived at the capital of Luoyang, and Emperor Gaozong treated him with great reverence. At that time, the Master was still a young child.

He prostrated before the Tripitaka Master and requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. The assembly said to the Tripitaka Master, "This youth is able to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and also understands its meaning.
The Tripitaka Master marveled and said, "The One Vehicle of the *Avataṃsaka* is the secret treasury of all Buddhas;

it is difficult even to encounter, let alone to master its meaning. If there were someone who could recite even the single chapter on 'Pure Conduct' from the *Avataṃsaka*, [they would be rare indeed]."
That person had already attained the full purity of the bodhisattva precepts and would not receive the bodhisattva precepts again.
During the Tian-shou era, while his teacher was lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, a Taoist priest uttered coarse words during a discussion concerning the heterodox and the orthodox.

The next morning, when he washed his face, both his eyebrows and hair fell out. Only then did he give rise to a heart of repentance, return to revere the Triple Gem, and vow to uphold the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
He had already completed one hundred recitations, yet before he had even finished ten more, his eyebrows and hair suddenly grew back.
In Zhongshan, Dingzhou of the Tang dynasty, there was Meditation Master Xiude, whose nature was formed by rigorous discipline and who dwelt in the mountains and forests to uphold the Way.

He specialized exclusively in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. In the fourth year of the Yonghui era, he resolved to transcribe it; he established a separate pure courtyard and planted mulberry trees for the purpose. After three...

The year [was such-and-such]. He bathed the manuscript with scented water and prepared the paper with purity. Furthermore, he constructed a separate altar of purification and summoned the skilled scribe Wang Gong of Weizhou.
Having fasted, bathed, and donned clean robes, they burned incense and scattered flowers, hanging up various banners and canopies while performing prostrations, reciting scriptures, and repenting.

Only then did they ascend the seat to write. As the brush was lowered, they held fragrant incense; as it was raised, they exhaled breath. This was done daily and consistently. The Master, meanwhile, entered his chamber to engage in meditative visualization.
For every scroll he transcribed, he offered ten bolts of silk, but Senggong would not accept them. Upon its completion, he assembled the congregation to hold a vegetarian feast in celebration.
Before the assembly, the Master burned incense, scattered flowers, and made great vows; as soon as he opened the scripture repository, a magnificent radiance was emitted.

It spans more than seventy *li* in circumference and illuminates the city of Dingzhou. The assembly gathered for the fast within the mountains, as well as the various men and women, cast themselves down in sorrowful repentance;
there were none who did not look up to him with reverence. This was recorded in the *Hui-xuan-ji*.

During the Shengli era of the Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda stated that in the kingdom of Kucha, people practiced only the Hīnayāna and were unaware that Śākyamuni had manifested billions of emanations, appearing as clouds of various bodies.

A Brahmin monk from India arrived in that country carrying the Sanskrit original of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, but the Hīnayāna masters there did not believe or accept it; consequently, the Brahmin monk remained behind.
Having passed through [the city], they returned home. The masters of the Hīnayāna then threw the sūtra into a well. Subsequently, the well emitted a brilliant light, blazing like a mass of fire.
That night, when the masters saw it, they suspected it was gold or treasure. When morning came, they sent someone to fish it out.

This was the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* that had been discarded previously. The masters were struck with wonder and amazement; they subsequently retrieved it and returned it to the scripture repository, placing it within the central niche.
Later, they suddenly saw this sūtra on the very top shelf of the repository. The masters said to one another, "This too is what was taught by our Śākyamuni.
I noticed there were slight discrepancies [in the previous version], so I placed it within the central niche of the repository. Who has dared to move it?"

The upper shelf was then moved aside, and a lower niche was placed there; the door was locked, and the keys were strictly guarded. When it was opened for inspection the following day, the image was found to have returned to its original position on the upper shelf.

Only then did the masters realize that the majestic spiritual power of the One Vehicle’s Great Teaching was such as this, and they repented their former lack of faith while beginning to admire it with devotion.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* subsequently flourished in various countries; this is seen in the *Biographies of Master Ying’s Spiritual Responses*.
The monk Huiyou of Chongfu Monastery during the Tang dynasty was rigorous and austere in his observance of the precepts. He served Master Yan and specialized exclusively in the *Avataṃsaka*.

Every dawn and on auspicious nights, he would burn incense and reverently recite the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata. Suddenly, he saw more than ten bodhisattvas emerge from [the light].
They emerged from the earth, manifesting golden bodies that all radiated light; sitting upon lotus seats, they joined their palms and listened to the recitation.
When the sutra was finished, they vanished.
Shi Daoying of the Tang dynasty, surnamed Chen of Puzhou, was eighteen years old when his parents arranged for him to marry. They lived together for five years.
"I vow never to offend you again. Later, he followed Dharma Master Ju of Bingzhou to hear the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and subsequently shaved his head.
He entered Baiti Monastery on Mount Taihang to practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Once, during a severe drought, he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to pray for rain.

Two old men appeared, each attended by two youths, who came at times to listen to the lecture. When Tanxuan questioned them about their extraordinary appearance, they replied: [The text continues with the response.]
He said, "Your disciples are all sea deities. Because they cherish this sutra, they have come to listen and receive it.
The Master said, "I am now lecturing on the sutra for you, the donor; please send down a light rain. The old man commanded his two youths, and the youths immediately emerged from the window opening.
In a short while, a great rain poured down in torrents, upon which those far and near all relied. The two old men bowed in thanks and suddenly vanished.

The National Teacher Qingliang of the Tang dynasty was named Chengguan, with the courtesy name Daxiu. He was of the Xiahou clan of Kuaiji and was born in the Wuyin year of the Kaiyuan era during the reign of Emperor Xuanzong.

He stood nine chi and four cun tall; his hands reached below his knees when hanging down, he had forty teeth in his mouth, and his eyes emitted light at night while remaining unblinking during the day.
In the second year of the Jianzhong era, he resided on Mount Wutai and began penning his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
One day he had a dream: a golden mountain rose majestically, its radiant form shimmering with brilliance. Upon waking, he knew this to be an omen of the Universal Radiance (Samantabhadra).
From then on, his pen never paused in its flow of thought; after four years, the text was completed.

Furthermore, he dreamed that he transformed himself into a dragon, its head raised at the Southern Terrace while its tail coiled around the Northern Terrace, twisting and turning as it soared through the void. In an instant, it multiplied into hundreds and thousands of forms, winding and gliding in azure splendor.

The ink dispersed in all four directions. Those who understood this took it as an omen of the widespread circulation [of his teachings]. When he first lectured for the assembly, auspicious clouds were moved to condense in the sky, circling about to form a canopy.

In addition to his commentaries and sub-commentaries, he further composed the *Shoujing* (Hand Mirror) in one hundred fascicles, the *Huayan Gangyao* (Essentials of the Avataṃsaka) in three fascicles, the *Zhengyao* (Essential Points) in one fascicle, the *Fajie Guan Xuanjing* (Mysterious Mirror of the Contemplation of the Dharma Realm) in one fascicle, and the *Jingdeng Shuowen* (Explanations of the Mirror Lamp) in one fascicle.

*The Three Sages’ Perfectly Interfused Contemplation*, one fascicle; *The Diagram of the Flower Treasury World from the Seven Locations and Nine Assemblies*, one fascicle; *The Exegesis of the Heart-Mirror*, ten fascicles.
During the Zhenyuan era, he was summoned by imperial decree to enter the inner palace, where he ascended the seat to expound the fundamental principles of the Avataṃsaka school.

Thereupon, the authorities were ordered to cast a seal for him, and he was promoted to the rank of National Teacher with the title Qingliang (Cooling). He passed away in the third month of the third year of the Kaicheng era. [His] birth...

His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on Mount Zhongnan. Not long after, a foreign monk arrived at the capital and submitted a memorial stating that he had seen two messengers at the Pamir Mountains who were passing through the air.
He used a mantra to stop them and questioned them; they replied, "The Mañjuśrī Hall in North India."
He was a divine being. He traveled east to retrieve the great tooth of the Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and returned to his country to offer it in worship.

By imperial decree, the stupa was opened; indeed, one tooth had vanished, and only thirty-nine remained. Thereupon, he was cremated. The śarīra were brilliant and translucent, and his tongue was like a red lotus.

He was subsequently posthumously titled National Preceptor Qingliang, and his memorial pagoda was named Miaojue. These details may be seen in the *Xùchāo Yuǎnqǐ xíngjì* (The Origin and Deeds of the Continued Commentary).
Shi Chenghuileng of the Tang dynasty was the son of the Li family of Qiu. His parents prayed at Mount Wutai before his birth.
Having grown up, he took leave of his parents and went to Zhenrong Monastery on Mount Wutai, where he received the tonsure under the Venerable Fashun.

He once recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in Liniugou, subsisting only on grasses and trees. Whenever he recited the sutra, five or seven men dressed in Confucian attire would sit and listen. He frequently maintained... [the text continues].

During the Yifeng era of the Tang dynasty, two Brahman monks from the Western Regions arrived at Mount Wutai.
Carrying flowers and holding incense burners, they crawled on their elbows and knees toward the mountain peak to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.

There they encountered a nun sitting upright and alone upon a rope bed beneath a pine tree amidst the rocky cliffs, reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. As evening was falling, the nun said to the Brahman monks: "I, the nun..."
"It would be appropriate for you to dwell together with the great Saṃgha. Venerable sir, please depart; come again tomorrow. The monk said, "The mountains are deep and the road is far;
I have nowhere to turn for shelter. What shall I do? The nun said, "If you do not go, I cannot remain here. I shall enter the deep mountains.
The monk lingered there, filled with shame and fear, not knowing where to go. The nun said, "Simply descend to the valley below; there is a meditation cave there. The monk—
They went to search for the cave where the fruit was obtained; it was some several *li* away. The two monks joined their palms, held incense burners, and faced north to pay distant homage.
With hearts fully inclined, they listened to the sutra, the sound of which reached their ears clearly.

When the title of the sutra was first opened, "Thus have I heard," they then saw from afar the nun’s body situated upon a rope-bed, sitting facing south. Light issued from her mouth, brilliant like the color of gold, shining brightly.
Before the peak, after she had recited more than two fascicles, the light became intense to the south of the valley, covering an area of about ten *li*, no different from daylight.
By the time she reached four fascicles, the light gradually withdrew; when the sixth fascicle was completed, the light was entirely drawn back into the nun’s mouth.

People considered this to be Mañjuśrī manifesting a transformation body to demonstrate his presence to the Indian monks. This is recorded in the *Yingshi Ganying Zhuan* (Biographies of Master Ying’s Spiritual Resonances).

During the Shangyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Sun Simiao consumed *liuzhudan* (flowing pearl elixir) and talc powder (*yunmufen*). At the age of one hundred and fifty, his countenance was like that of a youth.
When he arrived in Chang’an, he recounted events from the Qi and Wei periods as if he had witnessed them with his own eyes. He once transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
It comprised seven hundred and fifty fascicles. At that time, Emperor Taizong summoned him for an audience and asked which Buddhist scripture was the greatest.

Sun replied, "The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* is that which the Buddha held most highly. The Emperor said, "Recently, the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in six hundred fascicles;
why is it not considered the greatest? Why is it that only the eighty-fascicle *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* alone attains the title of 'Great'? Sun replied, "The *Avataṃsaka*..."
The Dharma-realm is majestic and complete with all gates; within a single gate, one may produce a great thousand-fold sutra-scroll.

The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is but a single gate within the *Avataṃsaka*. Only then did Emperor Taizong realize this, whereupon he took up and upheld the *Avataṃsaka*. This was seen in Master Ying’s *Account of Miraculous Responses*.
The Tang dynasty Master Li, whose courtesy name was Tongxuan, first arrived in Taiyuan and stayed at the home of Gao Shannu.

Every morning he consumed nothing but ten dates and a single *bǎiyè* (cypress leaf) cake. Later, he departed and encountered a tiger on the road; the beast lay submissive and docile, as if waiting for him.
The Master said to it, "I intend to compose a treatise to explain the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; you should select a location for me."
He took up residence there. A tiger carried the elder’s bag and bowl for over thirty li until they reached an earthen grotto, where it crouched and waited.
Once the elder entered the grotto, the tiger immediately tucked its tail and departed. Originally, there was no water in the grotto;

that evening, amidst wind and thunder, an ancient pine tree was uprooted, and a spring gushed forth from beneath it—crystal clear, sweet, and delicious. People of the time called it the "Elder’s Spring. Thereafter, the elder composed a treatise.

On that evening, his mind plumbed the depths of the profound mysteries, and from his mouth issued forth white light that illuminated the interior of the shrine-casket, serving as a substitute for lamps and candles.
At that time, there were two women of peerless beauty, their heads veiled with white cloth, who drew water for the Elder, burned incense, and provided paper and brushes.

Between the hours of Mārgaśīrṣa (卯) and Puṣya (辰), they would invariably prepare pure offerings, with every kind of sweet delicacy fully prepared. When the meal was finished and the vessels removed, no one knew [where they had come from].
He departed and traveled for five years. Just as he was nearing the completion of his treatise, he vanished without a trace. Regarding the history of the *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* by the Elder [Dushun]:
during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, Fan Xuanzhi, a native of Anding, knew how to cultivate the Way from a young age and took refuge with Dushun.
The Upādhyāya instructed him to take the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as his primary practice and to cultivate the conduct of Samantabhadra according to this scripture.
Whenever he recited the sutra, śarīras frequently emerged from his mouth; over time, there were several hundred grains. The *Biographies of Miraculous Responses of Dharma Master Huiying* states:
"On certain nights when the layman recited, golden light radiated from his mouth, illuminating an area of more than forty li. Those far and near were struck with wonder."
At the age of ninety-two, he passed away without illness. At the time of his cremation, his teeth were transformed into śarīras;
more than a hundred grains were obtained, all of which emitted light that did not cease for several days. Thereupon, both monastics and laypeople erected a stūpa to make offerings to them.
Tang Deng Yuanshuang was a native of Huayin. During the Zhengsheng era, a close relative of his died suddenly;
after seven days, he revived and recounted that he had been summoned from the underworld. Terrified, Yuanshuang was instructed by the man to transcribe the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

Once the transcription was complete, the Shu-qi葵花 (Hibiscus) planted beside Yuanshuang’s mother’s tomb—which had already withered by winter—suddenly burst into bloom, shining brilliantly and flourishing luxuriantly. The local community marveled at this wonder.
This was reported to the court, and he was honored with the designation of a "Gate of Filial Piety.

Furthermore, the *Huayan zhi* records that when Zou Ji was copying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, having reached halfway through the text, he suddenly saw a bhikṣu before his incense table. Zou asked, "Who are you to have come here?

He replied, "I am an attendant of the *Avataṃsaka*. Moved by your utmost sincerity, I have come specifically to grind the ink for you. Just as Zou was about to bow in thanks, [the monk] suddenly vanished.
Such are the spiritual responses resulting from copying the scriptures.
During the Yonglong era of the Tang dynasty, a man of Chang’an named Guo Shenliang, whose religious conduct was pure, suddenly died one day.
A celestial being led him to the Tuṣita Heaven palace, where he paid homage to Maitreya. One bodhisattva said to Guo: "Why do you not..."
When [Wang] Shouchi was upholding the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he replied, "Because there is no one to lecture upon it. The Bodhisattva said, "There is someone lecturing on it now;

Only then did he learn that Xianshou’s propagation of the Wheel of Dharma possessed such spiritual resonance and miraculous efficacy as this. This is recorded in the *Jianhui xuanyi*.
Chan Master Zu’jue of Zhongyan on Mount Emei in Song-dynasty Meizhou had mastered the scriptures by heart as a youth.

He composed a book to refute the teachings of Śākyamuni, but upon suddenly encountering an ominous vision, he repented and left the household life. He relied upon Chan Master Huimù Neng; not long after, an abscess broke out on his knee that remained incurable for five years despite medical treatment.

Consequently, he completed his *Huayan Helun* (Comprehensive Treatise on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra). One night he experienced a miraculous dream, and at dawn, he immediately relinquished [his previous views].
He walked with a steady gait. One day, while reciting the "Chapter on Manifesting Signs," he reached the passage:

"The Buddha-body has no birth, yet it can manifest birth; the nature of dharmas is like empty space, and all Buddhas dwell therein. Without dwelling and without departing, the Buddha is seen everywhere.

Thereupon, he attained realization of the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*. The provincial governor invited him to lecture at the Qianbu Hall; his words and meaning were grand and expansive, and the assembly...
All sighed in admiration and submission. This is recorded in the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.
During the Song dynasty, there was the Dharma Master Yuanjing, named Shengchang, of the Yan clan from Qiantang. He left home at the age of seventeen and received full ordination;

his observance of the precepts was meticulous and rigorous. He studied the Tiantai system of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight). During the Chunhua era, he took up residence at Zhaokong Temple, where he admired the spirit of Mount Lu.

Following this tradition, he established a society at West Lake. Taking the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the essential core for attaining sainthood, he drew blood from his own fingers to mix with ink and write it out.
For every single character he wrote, he would perform three prostrations, circumambulate three times, and recite the Buddha’s name three times.

Furthermore, he carved printing blocks and distributed one thousand volumes. He changed the name of the Lotus Society to the Society of Pure Conduct, and all those who joined the assembly were called "Pure Conduct" practitioners.
The disciples included the Duke Wenzheng Wang Dan and the State Councilor Xiang Minzhong as the leaders of the society.
There were one hundred and twenty scholar-officials of the time and one thousand bhikṣus. Su Yijian, of the Hanlin Academy, composed the preface to the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," in which he stated:
"I should spread my hair to receive his feet and gouge out my body to request his Dharma; even so, it would still not be enough."

How much less would I begrudge my own meager writings and shallow learning? On the first day of the first month in the fourth year of the Tianxi era, he sat upright, recited the Buddha’s name, and passed away;
he is thus regarded as the seventh patriarch of the Lotus Society.
The Song dynasty monk Shi Shanben attained ordination through an examination on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. He constantly recited and upheld [the scriptures] without ceasing.
By imperial decree, he resided at Fayun Monastery and was granted the title Chan Master Da Tong. Later, he returned to Xiangwu Temple in Hangzhou to cultivate the practice of Pure Land.

While in meditative concentration, he beheld Amitābha Buddha manifesting a golden body. One day, he told his disciples, "Three days from now, I shall depart. When the appointed time arrived, [he passed away].
He passed away while sitting in the lotus posture, facing west as he recited the Buddha’s name.
During the Yuanyou era of the Song dynasty, there was a monk from Shu named Dharma Master Zhichao, who had been constantly reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for thirty years.
He once happened to see a youth of exceptionally refined and extraordinary spirit, who raised his hand in a high bow. Zhichao asked him whence he came; the youth replied, "From Mount Wutai."
Chao said, "Why have you come from so far? He replied, "It is because I wish to instruct you on a minor matter.
While it is truly praiseworthy that your master recites the scriptures, there is a lapse regarding the time of using the latrine and performing purification.

When touching water to wash his hands, he merely rinses the backs of his hands with water and never uses ash or mud to wash them (or alternatively, soap-nut balls may be used). Regarding the ash and mud used for washing, the Vinaya regulations stipulate seven applications; yet now, only two are used."

Third: "If one continues to perform prostrations to the Buddha and recites scriptures while this contact still remains, one incurs sin in every instance. Having spoken these words, he vanished. Daochao felt ashamed and amended his ways.

Even for laypeople who recite and study, they too must practice in accordance with the Dharma. If they cannot do so..."
By reciting these verses and mantras, one may avoid the sin of irreverence. The verse for entering the latrine says:
