The mantra says: *Oṃ huluḍāya svāhā* (recite three times). The verse for cleansing after finishing says: "Having completed the task and approached the water, I vow that all sentient beings shall [swiftly attain] within the supramundane Dharma..."
Go quickly. Recite the mantra: *Oṃ hana-malite svāhā* (three times). The verse for removing impurities says:
"Washing away physical defilements, may all sentient beings become pure, harmonious, and ultimately stainless. Recite the mantra: *Oṃ śrīye bhahe svāhā* (three times).
The verse for cleansing the hands says: "Washing the palms with water, may all sentient beings attain purity."
[Place] the hands [in the gesture of] receiving and upholding the Buddha-dharma. Recite the mantra: *Oṃ jukāraye svāhā* (three times).
When the Song Dynasty’s Wenzhong Duke Ouyang was about to change his bedding before death, he called his children and disciples and admonished them, saying:

"In my youth, I was renowned for my literary works and strove to denounce the Buddhists. Lately, however, I have suddenly heard profound meanings within the various sutras; I am now about to investigate the True [Dharma]."

In the end, he did not expect his aspirations to remain unfulfilled as he passed away. "You all must not follow my example by speaking lightly of the similarities and differences between the Three Teachings.
He then had an old soldier borrow the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from a nearby temple; he chanted it with solemnity until reaching the eighth fascicle, at which point he sat peacefully and passed away.
Sūn Liáng of the Song dynasty was a native of Qiántáng. He lived in seclusion and studied the *Tripitaka*, attaining a profound mastery of the essential principles of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He constantly recited and upheld the scriptures without ceasing. Later, he relied upon the Vinaya Master Dàzhì to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. For nearly twenty years, he recited the Buddha’s name ten thousand times daily.
One day, he instructed his family to invite monks to perform the Buddha-recitation ceremony. After only half a meal’s time had passed, he joined his palms toward the void and said, "All..."
The Buddha has already accepted her descent; she passed away while sitting in retreat.
She was née Jingjian of the Qin family from Songjiang. Having grown weary of her female body, she lived separately from her husband and maintained the precepts and fasts with great diligence.
He constantly recited the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prabhāsa*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and other sutras without a single day of omission.
Morning and evening he prostrated before the Buddha and practiced the Amitābha repentance ritual. After a long time, a radiant light entered his room; facing west, he sat upright and passed away.
Suvarṇasūśrī was a monk from Nālandā Monastery in Central India who recited and upheld the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

At the age of eighty-five, he traveled by sea to pay homage at Mount Wutai. At each of the mountain peaks, he recited ten copies of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and practiced meditative stillness for seven days.
In meditative concentration, he beheld a golden city and a dark-blue palace, with precious lotuses in fragrant water and jeweled nets reflecting light in mutual brilliance;
celestial youths played and sported therein. Later, he passed away on Vulture Peak, leaving behind eight *he* of *śarīra* relics that were as brilliant and radiant as pearls.
This is recorded in the *Yunqi Ganying Lueji*.
The former Huayan Bodhisattva’s name was Zhengshun. He was the son of the Gao family from Weizhou.

Having received the tonsure under Master Yong of Shouning on Mount Wutai, he built a hut among the deep trees and devoted himself solely to reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, completing over a thousand fascicles. Whenever he entered the contemplation of the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang guan*), he would not emerge for three or five days;
thus, he was popularly known as the Huayan Bodhisattva. As he was about to pass away, his disciples requested a verse. The Master said: "Throughout..."
"Kalpas fundamentally have neither going nor staying. What need is there for thought or deliberation? Turning one's body, one tramples through empty space;

let all right and wrong be disregarded. Having spoken thus, he passed away. On that day, five-colored dragons appeared upon his spirit-tablet, their flying radiance illuminating the courtyard and halls.
This is recorded in the *Brief Account of Miraculous Responses at Yunqi*.
During the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, Chan Master Bianrong was cast into prison due to slanderous rumors.

The jailer, noting that Master Bian was highly renowned and certain to possess much gold, demanded a heavy bribe from him. The Master replied, "How could a monk have money? I have nothing at all to give.
The jailer then placed the Master inside a large wooden chest on a bed to confine him. When the chest was finally closed, the Master sang toward the void: "The Great Vaipulya..."
The *Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra* and the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the Avataṃsaka Assembly suddenly filled the box and bed, making a clamorous noise; the lock broke and the bed shattered.
When this incident was reported to the prison warden, it reached the Imperial presence. By imperial decree, he was invited to come forth. The *Two Brushes of Yunqi’s Bamboo Window* states:
"When I entered the capital, I went with my peers to visit Master Bianrong to pay our respects and seek his instruction. Rong instructed me as follows:"
He had no desire for profit, no quest for fame, and did not seek the patronage of the gates of the powerful or influential; he simply devoted his single mind to realizing the Way.
After he left, several young men laughed and said, "We thought he possessed some extraordinary learning; why is he so broad-minded and superficial?
I say that this is precisely where this old man is worthy of respect. Even though he was a blunt speaker, how could he not have gathered together the questions and answers of the former masters?
Regarding one or two instances of karmic conditions, he used them as a means of concealment; yet those who do not act thus speak only what they have actually practiced.
Teaching others by exemplifying his own conduct—this is the true and authentic Chan practitioner. One must not treat such a person with contempt.
Mingge, whose dharma name was Guangtai, was a native of Qiantang. He was profoundly filial by nature and had long accumulated virtuous deeds, yet he remained deeply humble and concealed his talents.

In his later years, he served the Buddha with sincere devotion; together with the Lingzhi monk Xuansu, he established two seasonal assemblies for the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) and the recitation of the five scriptures of the *Avataṃsaka*.
Later, he suddenly said to others: "My great life-limit is approaching; I shall depart for the West."

He returned to his provisions and subsequently entered retreat for recitation, never ceasing day or night. He predetermined that his date for returning would be the twenty-first day of the twelfth lunar month.
On the evening of the second day prior to that date, his wife and children surrounded him, weeping with choked voices. Go laughed and said, "Birth must inevitably end in extinction;

why should you grieve? I am now concentrating my spirit on the pure realm. You all must be careful not to disturb me with worldly attachments. When the appointed time arrived, he passed away peacefully.

However, he passed away soon after. Not long later, a monk entered the underworld and saw Sun sitting in meditation in a quiet room. Sacred texts filled his desk, and the courtyard was filled with purple bamboo and stone peaks;
it was as pristine and secluded as a celestial cavern (*dongtian*). This is recorded in the *Yunqi Wangsheng Ji* (The Collection on Rebirth at Yunqi).
The biography of Lady Yan, mother of Minister of Works Tan Zhengmo: In her daily management of the household and instruction of her sons, she maintained strict discipline and propriety.
Although her husband and son held high office, she wore plain clothes and ate simple vegetables, taking no pleasure in luxury or ostentation. By nature, she was fond of Buddhist teachings.

Morning and evening, he never ceased his ritual recitations of the *Vajracchedikā* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. In his later years, he especially revered the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, reciting one fascicle daily with consecrated empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Furthermore, he was able to explain its great principles to his son and daughter-in-law. Throughout his life, he suffered no illness. In the summer months of the *Ren-shen* year of the Chongzhen era, he suddenly fell ill;
knowing immediately that his end was near, he rose to bathe, changed his robes, and prostrated before the Buddha, saying: "I, one..."
He conceived a deep reverence for the Buddha. Because he possessed the karmic affinity for the Buddha, his physical remains did not emit any foul odor;

instead, they remained seated upright in the full lotus posture with palms joined as he passed away. For seven days, his countenance bore a smile as if he were still alive, and a fragrant aroma wafted forth from time to time.
Not a single fly alighted upon the funeral site, and all who saw it could not help but marvel at this wonder. There is a formal biographical record of these events by the Ministry of Works.
